title: The Tool Call That Cannot Fail Silently

questions.question: In the tool invocation lifecycle, what happens to a tools/call request after it is received but before its handler ever runs?
options: It is parsed, validated against the tool's declared schema, and only then routed to execution
It is executed immediately, and the result is checked against the schema only after the handler returns
It is queued until the next protocol version ships, since only that version defines its handler
It is forwarded unread to whichever client sent it, so the client can approve it first
questions.explanation: A request only reaches a handler after passing the parse and validate checkpoints; running the handler first and checking the schema afterward would let bad input reach the handler unguarded.

questions.question: When does an MCP server return a Parse error, code -32700, instead of some other JSON-RPC error?
options: When the tool named in the call's params has never been registered with this particular server
When the raw payload the transport delivered cannot be parsed as syntactically valid JSON at all
When a field the tool's input schema marks as required is missing from the arguments object
When the handler function bound to a registered tool raises an unhandled exception while it runs
questions.explanation: Parse error fires before the server can read a method or an id out of the message, because the payload never became valid JSON in the first place, which is why its id is reported as null.

questions.question: A client sends a tools/call request naming a tool the server never registered. Which JSON-RPC error should the server return?
options: Invalid params, because the arguments object failed to satisfy the tool's declared input schema
Invalid Request, because the JSON-RPC envelope was missing its version string or its id
Method not found, because there is nothing registered under that name for the server to run
Internal error, because the handler function threw an exception partway through running
questions.explanation: Method not found covers both an unrecognized top-level method and a tool name the server never registered, since in both cases there is simply nothing on the server to execute.

questions.question: A registered tool receives a call whose arguments object is missing a field its input schema marks as required. Which error fires, and at which checkpoint?
options: Method not found, at the validation checkpoint, because the server cannot route to an unknown tool
Parse error, at the parsing checkpoint, because the transport delivered text that was not valid JSON
Internal error, at the execution checkpoint, because the handler raised once it started running
Invalid params, at the validation checkpoint, because the schema check runs before the handler runs
questions.explanation: The tool itself was found, so this is not a routing failure; the missing field is caught by the schema check that runs during validation, before execution ever begins.

questions.question: A tool's handler divides by a number the caller supplied, and that number turns out to be zero. What should a conformant MCP server do?
options: Catch the exception the handler raised and return Internal error, code -32603, instead of crashing
Let the whole process crash, since a caller that sends zero deserves an unhandled exception
Retry the same handler call automatically until the division happens to stop raising
Return a result object containing the raw Python traceback text as the answer
questions.explanation: A handler exception is a runtime failure no schema could have caught in advance, so the server must catch it and translate it into a structured error rather than letting the process crash or leaking implementation detail.

questions.question: Why does every JSON-RPC response from an MCP server, whether it carries a result or an error, repeat the id of the request it answers?
options: So the client can print the id somewhere in a log file kept for later review
So the client can match each response to the request that produced it in the first place
So the server can charge a fee to the caller proportional to how far the call got
So the transport layer knows how many bytes to compress before sending back the response
questions.explanation: A client may have several requests outstanding at once, and the id is the only thing that lets it tell which outstanding call a given result or error belongs to, whether that call succeeded or failed at some checkpoint.
